nodes.label: Per-event judgment: signal (choice of six)
nodes.rationale: Jev choice question with six options: competitor, escalation, champion_exit, stall, momentum, routine. The SIGNALS criteria are the exact strings both Jev and Claude receive, and they carry the edge cases: a competitor named only to be rejected is momentum, someone other than the champion leaving is routine, and a champion promoted inside the account is momentum. Scores: Jev 91.8% per event and 89.0% per deal, Haiku 91.8%, Sonnet 87.7% per event and 90.4% per deal.

nodes.label: Per-event judgment: severity (score over none, watch, serious, critical)
nodes.rationale: Jev score question over four ordered levels. Each event is judged on its own with the deal record as context, and good news is always none. jev.read() rounds Jev's continuous score to the nearest level. Exact match: Jev 67.1% per event and 63.0% per deal, every Claude setup 87.7%. Within one level every setup is 97.3% or better.

nodes.label: Per-event judgment: exec_engaged (noul, did a senior customer person take part)
nodes.rationale: Jev noul question: did a senior customer person (VP and above, any C-level title, President or Founder) actively speak, write, decide or edit in this event? Directors, heads of department, managers and leads do not count, and neither does being cc'd, mentioned or changing jobs. The probability is cut at 0.5 and the raw p_exec is kept for the Brier score. It carries the most money because it drives no_exec_30d. Per event, Jev, Haiku and Sonnet all score 94.5%. Per deal, Jev and Sonnet both reach 98.6% (Brier 0.009 and 0.016).

nodes.label: Risk reason: competitor
nodes.rationale: Two or more competitor events at watch or worse, or one critical. Printed as 'competitor mentioned xN'. Ironbridge ($240K) and Keystone ($210K) carry it in the answer key.

nodes.label: Risk reason: escalations
nodes.rationale: Two or more escalation events at serious or worse, or one critical. Printed as 'N tickets escalated'. Cloudmark ($94K) and Precision ($62K).

nodes.label: Risk reason: champion_left
nodes.rationale: A champion_exit event at serious or worse. Printed as 'champion left'. Only Vantage ($128K) has it, and both champion_exit events in the set are Vantage's, so treat results on this class as an anecdote.

nodes.label: Risk reason: stalled
nodes.rationale: A stall event at serious or worse: budget cut or frozen, seats reduced, or the deal pushed out. Printed as 'budget or timing slipped'. Halcyon ($150K) and Tidewater ($76K).

nodes.label: Risk reason: no_exec_30d
nodes.rationale: The deal is worth $100K or more and no exec_engaged event falls in the 30 days before as_of. No single event can show it. It only exists across the whole ledger, which is why it lives in code. Datacore ($185K) is the answer-key case. The ledger run's six false alarms, Jev per deal's Silverline alarm and the review step's Datacore mistake all involve this rule.

nodes.label: Risk reason: closing_with_issues
nodes.rationale: The deal closes within 7 days of as_of and at least one event is serious or worse. Printed as 'closes in Nd with open issues'. Precision, closing 2026-09-28, is the only case.

nodes.label: RISK_RULES: the deal risk rule written in words
nodes.rationale: The same six-reason rule as spec.assess(), written in words with the bracketed reason keys, the $100K threshold and the 30-day window. The claude-sonnet-5-ledger setup and the brief.py review prompt get this text and have to apply it themselves. Every other setup hands its event labels to spec.assess().

nodes.label: COMPETITORS: invented competitor names (Hexline, Corvid, Tallyworks)
nodes.rationale: Made up so no real product ends up in a synthetic loss report, and both models are told the names up front. Week 01 showed Jev cannot be expected to know who a company's competitors are, and week 02 is not testing that. The README credits this for the task being easier than week 01.
